Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology of total hip and knee arthroplasty and its implications.
Delineate and describe the various types of private and public insurance providers.
Assess the history and status of the Affordable Care Act.
Describe the premise of accountable care organizations and how they have affected specialty
care.
Describe various alternative payment models and distinguish between the Bundled Payments
for Care Improvement Initiative of 2013, the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement
Model, and the Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced Initiative.
Define the Stark Law and the Physician Payments Sunshine Act.

Background: Healthcare Spending and Epidemiology of Total
Joint Arthroplasty
In 2018, healthcare spending accounted for nearly 18% of the gross domestic product, with
this figure continuing to rise. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) predicted
national spending growth to occur at a mean annual rate of 5.4%.
The largest diagnosis-related group (DRG) payment by CMS to hospitals in 2008, accounting for
4.6% of payments, was for total joint replacement (DRG 470); therefore arthroplasty is of
interest to policymakers looking to reduce costs.
The number of primary total hip and total knee arthroplasty procedures performed each year
is growing in a linear fashion; consequently, the revision burden also is rising.

Background: Healthcare Spending and Epidemiology of Total Joint
Arthroplasty
Healthcare spending accounted for nearly 18% of the gross domestic product in the
United States in 2018 and increases annually. The US healthcare system is notorious for
higher spending despite inferior population-wide health outcomes and worse access to
care than other wealthy countries. Cost containment is a continuing challenge given an
aging population and a lack of emphasis on value. In a recent National Health
Expenditure Projection for 2019 to 2028, CMS predicted national health spending to
grow at a mean annual rate of 5.4% from 2019 to 2028, reaching $6.2 trillion by 2028,
with Medicare expected to experience the fastest spending growth during that period
(7.6% per year).1 These expenditures will outpace the growth of the US gross domestic
product by a mean of 1.1 percentage points per year.
Although all medical specialties are subject to scrutiny and reform efforts focused on
cost containment, orthopaedic surgery—specifically arthroplasty—represents an easy
target for policy makers given that the largest DRG payment by CMS to hospitals in 2008
was for total joint replacement (DRG 470), which accounted for 4.6% of payments.2 This
is particularly relevant because predictive models anticipate a considerable increase in
primary and revision total hip and knee arthroplasty. Sloan et al3 reported that linear,

rather than exponential, projection models better characterized the growth of total joint
arthroplasty in the United States (Figure 1). Despite these relatively more conservative
projections, their models predicted that, by the year 2030, the volume of total hip
arthroplasty (THA) procedures would increase 71.2% and the volume of total knee
arthroplasty (TKA) procedures would increase 84.9%. This rising demand for primary TKA
will concordantly result in an increased economic burden of revision TKA, projected to
surpass $13 billion annually by the year 2030, particularly given younger and younger
patients undergoing total joint arthroplasty4-6 (Figure 2). Similarly, more than 50,000
revision THA procedures are performed annually in the United States, amounting to a $1
billion expenditure, with the frequency of revision THA projected to double by the year
2026.6,7 Consequently, orthopaedic surgeons are well poised to be critical players in the
discourse about and implementation of healthcare reform focused on incentivizing high-
value, patient-centered care (Resource 1).

Insurance Providers
Public insurance coverage includes Medicare, Medicaid, military and Veterans Affairs
programs, the Indian Health Service, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program.
Medicare has four parts. Patients are eligible for it if they are 65 years or older and have paid
into Medicare for at least 10 years, have certain disabilities, or have end-stage renal disease.
Medicaid is available for low-income individuals and is funded federally and by states;
however, eligibility is determined at the state level.
Private insurance options include health maintenance organizations (HMOs), point-of-service
providers, preferred provider organizations, high-deductible coverage, and health savings
accounts.

Insurance Providers
According to the 2019 census, 92% of Americans had health insurance coverage. Of
those individuals, 68% had private health insurance compared with 34% who had public
coverage, with employment-based insurance being the most common subtype (55.4%)8 (
Figure 3).
Figure 3 Bar graph shows the percentage of people by type of health insurance coverage

Keisler-Starkey K, Bunch LN: U.S. Census Bureau Current Population Reports P60-271:
Health Insurance Coverage in the United States, 2019. Washington, DC, US Government
Publishing Office, September 2020.)

Public Coverage
Public coverage includes Medicare (21%), Medicaid (16%), and military/Veterans Affairs
programs, as well as other smaller programs, such as the Indian Health Service and the
Federal Employees Health Benefits Program. Out-of-pocket spending grew 2.8% in 2018
to $275.6 billion, which was faster than the 2.2% growth rate observed in 2017. The CMS
is a subdivision of the US Department of Health and Human Services that tracks

Medicare and Medicaid were established by the Social Security Act Amendments of 1965,
signed into effect by President Lyndon B. Johnson. Since their inception, the programs
have undergone substantial modification and currently represent a substantial portion
of healthcare coverage. Medicare provides healthcare coverage for:
(1) individuals aged 65 years or older
(2) individuals younger than 65 years with certain disabilities
(3) individuals of all ages with end-stage renal disease
Medicare consists of four parts labeled A, B, C, and D.
Medicare

Medicare
Medicare Part A represents hospital insurance and covers expenses related to
inpatient care in hospitals and skilled nursing facilities, as well as some hospice
and home health care if beneficiaries meet certain criteria. The skilled facility
coverage applies only to posthospitalization coverage within 30 days of a
hospitalization that lasts at least 3 days. All individuals aged 65 years or older
are eligible for benefits given that they paid into the Medicare trust fund for 10
or more years (40 quarters). Most people covered by Part A do not pay a
premium because they or their spouse paid for it via their payroll taxes while
working.
Medicare Part B is medical insurance that partially covers physician services,
outpatient care, and various home health care services. It also covers some
additional medical services not included in Part A, including physical therapy
and laboratory work. Most people pay a monthly premium for Part B. The
standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B enrollees in 2019 was $135.50;

Medicare Part C, otherwise known as the Medicare Advantage Plan, provides all
Part A and Part B coverage and additional coverage extending to vision, hearing,
and dental care. These auxiliary plans are purchased through Medicare-
approved private companies and charge various out-of-pocket fees. Medicare
Part C has been increasing in popularity, with more than one-third (36%) of all
Medicare beneficiaries being enrolled in Medicare Advantage Plans in
202011 (Figure 5). According to the Kaiser Family Foundation, most Medicare
Advantage enrollees are in plans operated by United HealthCare, Humana, or
BlueCross BlueShield (Figure 6), and, as of 2020, nearly two-thirds of enrollees
paid no premium11 (Figure 7).

Medicaid
Medicaid is the other major public insurance program, which is available to certain low-
income individuals and families. Unlike Medicare, which is funded at the federal level,
Medicaid is partly funded by the federal government and partly funded by the state.
Therefore, eligibility requirements are dictated by the state but generally are determined
by age, pregnancy status, disability, and/or income. Medicaid eligibility for children is
assessed independent of the parent’s eligibility. Total Medicaid spending accelerated in
2018 to an expenditure of $597.4 billion, which represents a 3% increase compared with
2017. Medicaid spending on a per-enrollee basis was $8,201 in 2018.9

Private Insurer Models
Various commercial health insurance products exist, and they can be purchased by
individuals or through employers. Some models include traditional fee-for-service,
managed care, and consumer-directed health programs. Common models include
HMOs, preferred provider organizations, point-of-service care, high-deductible plans,
and health savings accounts.
Health Maintenance Organizations

Health Maintenance Organizations
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Economics of Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000018
11/30

HMOs are managed care programs that provide integrated coverage for
patients. Patients are cared for by providers employed by the HMO or by
providers in separate groups that are contracted with the HMO and typically
practice in the HMO facilities. HMOs emphasize preventive medicine, and access
to specialty services often requires a referral from primary care providers. The
insurance company dictates the services for which it pays; controls the cost of
those payments (often via prospective payment models); and often shares
financial risk with physicians, health systems, and patients. Although these
generally are positive characteristics, a disadvantage of HMOs is that the cost to
the patient may rise considerably if care from an out-of-network provider or
system is pursued.
Preferred Provider Organizations

Preferred Provider Organizations
Preferred provider organizations are a version of a managed care program.
Typically, employees are given a list of physicians and healthcare facilities
selected by their employer. An employee who goes to one of the designated
providers pays less than that for an out-of-network provider. The providers and
facilities typically are independent, and the primary care provider is not
required to be a gatekeeper for specialty services.
High-Deductible Health Plans

High-Deductible Health Plans
High-deductible health plans, otherwise referred to as catastrophic health plans,
are an option that provide insurance after a patient has reached a predefined
amount of healthcare spending out of pocket. These plans are most enticing for
individuals who typically do not require routine use of considerable medical
SEND FEEDBACK

resources but who want coverage if those resources are needed at a greater
level that exceeds the individual’s higher deductible.
Health Savings Accounts

Health Savings Accounts
Health savings accounts were established in 2003 as part of the Medicare
Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act and give individuals
and employers the option to contribute resources dedicated to health care with
certain tax benefits. The predetermined untaxed funds must be directed toward
health care, and any remaining funds can be carried over at the end of the year.
In general, health savings accounts dovetail nicely with high-deductible plans.
For 2019, an individual enrolled in a high-deductible plan could contribute
$3,500 for an individual or up to $7,100 for a family.12 In general, health savings
account funds may not be used to pay insurance premiums.
Healthcare Reform
The Affordable Care Act (ACA) was started in 2010 with the original goals of expanding access
to insurance, increasing consumer protections, improving preventative and wellness care
programs, and limiting federal health costs.
Accountable care organizations (ACOs) are a product of the ACA. They were created as a
means of streamlining care and reducing redundant medical expenditures for Medicare
recipients to improve patient care and lower costs in the traditional fee-for-service structure.
Alternative payment models germane to THA and TKA include the Bundled Payments for Care
Improvement (BPCI) Initiative, the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) Model, and
the BPCI Advanced Initiative.

Affordable Care Act

Affordable Care Act
The ACA was signed into law on March 23, 2010, by President Barack Obama. The three
primary goals of the ACA include making health care insurance affordable to more
individuals through subsidies, expanding the Medicaid program to cover all adults with
income below 138% of the federal poverty level, and supporting innovative medical care
delivery methods aimed at lowering the costs of health care. The ACA represented the
greatest healthcare overhaul since the introduction of Medicare and Medicaid in 1965;
however, its ability to effect lasting change or reform remains unclear because it was
built on unpartisan ground and remains a controversial topic, with a fate that may be
affected by the composition of the federal legislative bodies.
In its entirety, the ACA encompasses more than 900 pages of healthcare reform
measures directed toward expanding access to insurance, increasing consumer
protections, bolstering prevention and wellness programs, increasing the primary care
workforce, improving quality, and limiting federal healthcare costs. A major focus is
shifting care from emergency room visits to preventative and primary care and,
therefore, driving cost savings. Access to insurance coverage is garnered by requiring
employers to either cover employees (with the help of tax credits) or pay a fine;
mandating that individuals have health insurance (with the help of federal subsidies) or
face tax penalties; and enabling children to remain on their parents’ coverage until aged
26 years. Medicaid expansion to higher income levels also is supported through federal
subsidies; however, the Supreme Court ruled in 2012 that the ACA cannot require
Medicaid expansions13 (Figure 8). As of this writing, 12 states have not expanded
Medicaid with federal money and two states have adopted but not yet implemented the
expansion14 (Figure 9).

Under the ACA, hospitals and physicians also have been encouraged to form ACOs that
jointly contract care to certain populations of Medicare recipients in an effort to reduce
costs and to improve the quality of health care.
Funding for the ACA has been an ongoing source of contention. At its inception, the ACA
was to be funded in part by an increase in Medicare taxes on individuals making
$200,000 annually or joint filers making more than $250,000 annually. Tax penalties
imposed on individuals for not buying insurance, taxes on insurance companies, and
penalties paid by larger businesses who did not provide employee coverage also were
implemented. These mandates, particularly on those imposed on individuals, were met
with staunch opposition; however, the Supreme Court ruled them constitutional in 2012.
Five years later, the Congress repealed the individual mandate provisions of the ACA in a

tax bill. As of 2019, the repeal of the individual mandate had contributed to a 0.3%
decline in the number of individuals enrolled in private health insurance.1
The effect of the ACA can be evaluated generally and specifically with regard to patient
access to specialty providers, which is relevant to orthopaedics. Before the ACA,
approximately 45 million Americans were uninsured, representing approximately 18% of
the population. By 2016, that number decreased to 27 million, or approximately 10.9% of
Americans. The most recent data from 2019 revealed that only 9.6% of Americans
remained uninsured; however, it is not universally true that the increase in insurance
translates to a concomitant increase in access to care. Although primary care and
emergency services have improved for newly insured Americans, in part because of the
ACA requiring that primary care payments for Medicaid increase to Medicare levels,
access to specialty providers has not increased proportionally. Because Medicaid
provider rates are relatively undervalued, providers performing elective treatment
generally are less inclined to accept Medicaid patients. In a compelling study performed
in 2018, investigators contacted 93 orthopaedic practices to make a simulated Medicaid
appointment. Only 18.3% of practices offered an appointment, which represented 13.3%
of the orthopaedic surgeons in the study group. After the researchers removed safety-
net facility surgeons from the analysis, the number of practices offering a new
appointment was reduced considerably, to only 7.1%.15 Therefore, despite an absolute
reduction in uninsured visits after the implementation of the ACA, whether the act will
achieve an overall economic benefit given the asymmetric pressures on safety-net
institution or whether the increase in visits of newly insured patients will translate into
more surgical procedures or improved orthopaedic outcomes remain unclear.
Accountable Care Organizations

Accountable Care Organizations
The creation of ACOs was one of the first delivery-reform initiatives implemented under
the ACA. The goal was improve the historically fragmented and redundant US healthcare
system. The CMS defines ACOs as a group of doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Economics of Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000018
17/30

providers who come together voluntarily to provide coordinated high-quality care to
Medicare patients (Resource 2).
ACOs are an iteration of value-based payment reforms, in which providers are held
accountable by assuming performance risks—the risks for factors they can directly
influence (eg, the quality and cost of care they provide for their patients). ACOs give
hospitals and providers an opportunity to share in Medicare savings achieved by the
delivery of higher-value—rather than higher-cost—health services despite still
functioning in a largely fee-for-service world. Therefore, the ability to effectively function
within such a system would require an institutional commitment to creating systems to
provide cost-effective care.16 ACOs can be physician-led, composed of one or more
affiliated hospitals, or composed of an integrated delivery system.
The focus of efforts among ACOs has been cost reduction in the primary and post–acute-
care spheres. Many ACOs continue to struggle to save money in the realm of specialist
physician care. Some ACOs use cost-reduction measures to determine specialist
compensation. Although these groups reported marginally higher cost savings of $82.60
per beneficiary year, these were not statistically significant compared with findings
among ACOs not using cost-reduction–based specialists.17 ACOs have not been the
panacea for Medicare costs as many people hoped, particularly in the subspecialty
arena.
Alternative Payment Models

Alternative Payment Methods
Alternative payment models are the product of recent healthcare reforms aimed at
incentivizing value over volume. Traditional fee-for-service payment models reward
providers for performing more services, even if a reciprocal improvement in patient
outcomes does not occur. The three main models relevant to orthopaedics include the
BPCI Initiative of 2013, the Comprehensive CJR Model, and the BPCI Advanced Initiative.

BPCI Initiative

BPCI Initiative
The BPCI Initiative was authorized as part of the ACA and was piloted by CMS in 2013
with the goal of incentivizing providers to offer quality care at lower costs. Under the
BPCI program, CMS would pay one lump-sum payment for an entire episode of care
across 48 different inpatient DRGs. Some of the DRGs included were those for THA, TKA,
cervical fusion, and femur fracture fixation. Historical averages for a particular facility’s
Medicare beneficiaries in addition to a national trend factor are used to determine the
target payment allotment and are periodically reset. Participants either share in the
profits derived from coming in below the target price or are held financially accountable
for exceeding the target price in patients with higher costs of care. Most BPCI
participants assumed risk for the 90-day episode of care in some fashion but were able
to choose from one of four models with varying episode lengths and tiers of risk. Early
results from BPCI programs in total joint arthroplasty and spine surgery have been
reported.18-23 Courtney et al20 reported that for revision arthroplasty patients, although
the bundle group was associated with lower index inpatient admission costs, no
statistically significant difference was observed in overall costs (Table 1). Despite several
reports illustrating positive results in terms of cost reduction, reduced postacute care
utilization, and reduced readmission rates, concerns have been raised about alternative
payment models’ disincentivizing institutions to take on higher-risk patients and about
the need to implement risk-adjustment tools to offset the inclusion of these patients.24-
26 Patients at increased risk for complications because of multiple comorbidities, lower
socioeconomic status, or less social support may be viewed as bundle busters and may
consequently face access-to-care problems in the BPCI model. In addition, concern exists
that target price reductions may become unsustainable, at best making the ability for
institutions to share in profits nearly impossible and at worst penalizing institutions that
have been able to consistently control costs. Krueger et al26 published a series of studies
showing that, despite caring for more medically complex patients, their institution was
able to considerably decrease the rate of discharge to rehabilitation facilities (23% versus
14%) and the hospital length of stay (2.1 versus 1.7 days) without a change in
readmission rates. However, despite achieving a reduction in postacute care and 90-day

Comprehensive CJR Model

Comprehensive CJR Model
The Comprehensive CJR Model is a bundled-payment program for THA and TKA initiated
by CMS in April 2016. CMS mandated that nearly 800 hospitals in 67 metropolitan
statistical areas participate in this new value-based payment model. The Comprehensive
CJR Model differs from the BPCI Initiative in several ways. Unlike the flexibility afforded
by the BPCI Initiative and its four different models of varying episode lengths and levels
of risk, the Comprehensive CJR Model gives providers only one option. In addition,
instead of setting target prices based on the hospital’s historical performance, the

more resource utilization. Only hospitals under the Comprehensive CJR Model can
participate in the Comprehensive CJR Model bundles, whereas the remainder of
physician practices have the option of managing their own bundle with CMS through the
BPCI Initiative. The lack of physician input into these alternative payment models has
spurred criticism from orthopaedic surgeons.
BPCI Advanced Initiative

BPCI Advanced Initiative
The success of the BPCI program inspired the private sector to initiate several of its own
bundled-payment agreements to align incentives and reduce episode-of-care costs. Data
regarding the outcomes of these private-sector agreements are limited because of
protected information. In October 2018, CMS launched its new version of the BPCI
Initiative, the BPCI Advanced Initiative, which will run through 2023. Although it shares
many features of the original BPCI Initiative, it also includes three new bundle options
(bariatric surgery, transcatheter aortic valve replacement, and seizures); it streamlines all
care from day of discharge from the hospital through 90 days post-discharge; and its
participants are at risk for as much as 20% of the final target price. Perhaps most
importantly, the BPCI Advanced Initiative will qualify as an advanced alternative payment
model, enabling orthopaedic surgeons to earn bonus payments, which can be made only
via the Merit-based Incentive Payment System or via participation in an advanced
alternative payment model (ie, Comprehensive CJR Model or the BPCI Advanced
Initiative).27
Although not perfect, the paradigm shift from traditional fee-for-service models to those
incentivizing quality of care and value shows promise. A healthcare culture valuing
patient safety, efficient care, and quality improvement should continue to be a part of
healthcare reform, and physician leadership will be essential in ensuring that changes
are positive for patients and physicians. For example, the American Academy of

Legislation
The Stark Law is an antikickback law prohibiting physicians from referring Medicare or
Medicaid patients to an entity with which they or anyone in their immediate family has a
financial relationship.
The Stark Law is being called into question in the era of ACOs and alternative payment models
because it makes it harder to coordinate care in regions with fewer options.
The Physician Payment Sunshine Act requires physician compensation from industry to be
reported and to be made publicly available.
Stark Law

Stark Law
The germaneness of the Stark Law has recently been called into question in the era of
value-based reform. The Stark Law is essentially an antikickback law that prohibits a
physician from referring Medicare or Medicaid patients to an entity with which the
physician or an immediate family member has a financial relationship. The law
encompasses healthcare entities such as home healthcare services, durable medical
equipment, and physical and occupational therapy. Penalties for Stark Law violations
may be harsh and may include denial of payment, demand for reimbursement of
payments, and civil penalties for improper claims. Monitoring of referrals may be a
considerable burden on smaller healthcare facilities and may present challenges for
providers in regions with fewer referral options.29 Therefore, many are calling for
reexamination of the Stark Law, particularly now that US health care is moving away
from fee-for-service payments and moving toward value-based payment systems. The

introduced in Congress in April 2019, calls for the exemption of certain alternative
payment models under Medicare from the general prohibition on physician self-referrals

providers should know, understand, and follow the Stark Law.
Physician Payments Sunshine Act

Physician Payments Sunshine Act
The Physician Payments Sunshine Act, also known as Section 6002 of the ACA, requires
medical product manufacturers to disclose to CMS any payments or other transfers of
value made to physicians or teaching hospitals. Although the Physician Payments
Sunshine Act applies to all types of physicians, familiarity with its nuances is particularly
important for orthopaedic surgeons given that they regularly interact with industry. A
myriad of implant choices is available, and many surgeons choose their device
companies based on familiarity with a certain device or product throughout training or
because their institution’s agreements or pricing limit their choices. However, surgeons
also can assume consulting relationships with industry that may present conflicts of
interest. In addition, as new technology is introduced, industry is eager to fund training
and educational programs to familiarize surgeons with their devices. Although there is
nothing wrong with exploring new technology or different implants, surgeons must
understand the Physician Payments Sunshine Act so they are aware that the reporting is
happening and that it is publicly available. Items that are reported include:
(1) General payments (eg, cash and cash equivalents, honoraria, speaker fees, meals,
education, and grants)
(2) Ownership or investment interests held by physicians or their immediate family

Conclusion

Conclusion
The US healthcare system has undergone some of the most substantial reforms in its
history during the past decade, and continued changes can be expected. The shifting
focus toward quality over quantity is a positive one; however, physician leadership must
have a seat at the table during conversations about bundled-payment initiatives, quality
improvement strategies, and physician reimbursement. Healthcare settings and delivery
methods also are changing and are of particular interest to orthopaedic surgeons,
including the movement of surgical procedures out of large hospitals and academic
centers and into orthopaedic specialty hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers. Total
joint arthroplasty, which only a decade ago resulted in multiple-day inpatient admissions
and postacute care in a rehabilitation facility, is now routinely being performed on an
outpatient or extended-stay basis, with most patients being discharged home.
Orthopaedic surgeons perform quality-of-life–restoring procedures that are valued by
patients, and these physicians must remain vocal during conversations regarding policy
change so that they maintain access to care for patients, are compensated fairly, and are
adequately supported by the healthcare system.
